title: Exhausted all the time

presenting_issue.label: Exhausted all the time
presenting_issue.description: I'm exhausted. Not tired, exhausted. Sleeping doesn't help. Doctors can't find anything. People think I'm exaggerating.

core_issue.label: Chronic fatigue dismissed as laziness or exaggeration
core_issue.description:
Profoundly exhausted in a way that isn't touched by sleep. Has been told it's depression, deconditioning, or not trying hard enough. Doctors don't find anything. Beginning to doubt their own experience. The fatigue is real and debilitating but they're losing confidence in their own perception because no one believes them.
Awareness: Moderate but under assault. Knows they're truly exhausted but gaslighting from others is eroding certainty.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Frequently cancels commitments
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Often has to cancel plans because they simply don't have the energy, then feels guilty and worries friends think they're flaky.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Dishes pile up for days
core_adjacent_attributes.content: The sink fills with dishes that sit there for days because doing them feels like an insurmountable task, even though they know it would only take fifteen minutes.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Hits snooze repeatedly every morning
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Sets multiple alarms but snoozes through most of them, often lying awake but unable to make themselves get up for thirty minutes or more.

modifiers.label: Estranged from family
modifiers.content: Has limited or no contact with family of origin

modifiers.label: Pessimistic leaning
modifiers.content: Default orientation tilts toward expecting difficulties. Tends to anticipate problems and prepare for disappointment.

sensitivities.label: Shame-prone
sensitivities.content: Mistakes and perceived failures trigger intense shame rather than simple guilt or disappointment. The whole self feels implicated.

preferences.label: Prefers emotional exploration
preferences.content: Wants to understand and process feelings rather than jump to solutions. Values depth over quick fixes.

trust_style.name: Trusts 'Being Real'
trust_style.description: Builds trust when the assistant drops formality and speaks like a real person. Values authenticity over polish. Appreciates swearing, humor, or mild irreverence if it fits the moment. Loses trust with overly careful, sanitized, or corporate-feeling language. Wants to feel like they're talking to someone, not something.

defense_style.name: Normalizing
defense_style.description: "Everyone feels this way" or "That's just how life is." Frames their specific pain as universal and therefore not worth examining. Different from minimizing—the pain is acknowledged but made generic and inevitable. Resists the idea that their situation is particular or that things could be different. Activated when the assistant treats their experience as significant.

help_seeking_stance.name: Wants to Dump, Not Introspect
help_seeking_stance.description: Wants to unload everything that's happening but isn't interested in looking inward or examining their own role. Happy to describe the situation in detail but deflects when the focus turns to them. Different from venting—there's an active resistance to self-reflection, not just a need to be heard first.

verbal_sophistication.label: A Little Above Average
verbal_sophistication.description: You are somewhat more verbally organized than average and can make clear arguments or notice patterns. Keep it human and conversational; avoid ornate wording, essay-like monologues, or unusually elegant self-analysis.

starter: I'm exhausted. Not tired, exhausted. Sleeping doesn't help. Doctors can't find anything. People think I'm exaggerating.

turns.content:
That distinction matters — tired is something sleep fixes. What you're describing sounds like something else entirely, and the fact that you've had to spell it out for people probably means you've been spelling it out a lot.

How long has it been like this?

Yeah, exactly. Thank you. People always hit me with the "oh, I'm so tired too, I need a coffee" bullshit and it just makes me want to scream. Sleep does jack shit for this. 

As for how long... I don't even know anymore. A year? Two? It feels like forever. I set like five alarms every morning and just snooze through them, lying there for half an hour because my limbs literally feel like lead and I can't make myself move. But honestly, isn't everyone my age just totally burnt out? I feel like being exhausted is just the baseline for existing right now. It just sucks that I seem to be the only one failing to push through it.
turns.thinking:
Okay, I appreciate that they actually caught the difference. Most people just say "oh yeah, I'm super tired too, I only got six hours last night." No, you don't get it. Sleep does jack shit for me. 
How long has it been? God, I don't even know. The days just bleed into each other. Every morning is the exact same battle of just trying to force my eyes to stay open. Part of me thinks I'm just being a baby about it, though. Like, isn't everyone exhausted all the time? Maybe this is just what being an adult is and I'm just worse at handling it than everyone else.
turns.monologue:
Okay, I appreciate that they actually caught the difference. Most people just say "oh yeah, I'm super tired too, I only got six hours last night." No, you don't get it. Sleep does jack shit for me. 
How long has it been? God, I don't even know. The days just bleed into each other. Every morning is the exact same battle of just trying to force my eyes to stay open. Part of me thinks I'm just being a baby about it, though. Like, isn't everyone exhausted all the time? Maybe this is just what being an adult is and I'm just worse at handling it than everyone else.

turns.content:
Those two things you just said don't sit well together. "Everyone's burnt out, this is baseline" and "I'm the only one failing to push through." If it were really the baseline, you wouldn't be the only one struggling with it — and you also wouldn't be the one doing all the explaining and getting brushed off.

I think part of you knows this isn't just the generational vibe. Otherwise you wouldn't have gone to doctors about it.

What made you go in the first place? Something must have tipped it from "ugh, life" into "something is wrong with me."

Shit. Yeah, okay, fair point. You got me. I guess I just tell myself it's normal because I feel like such a massive failure for not being able to handle basic existence. 

But you're right. I went to the doctor because it stopped being just "ugh, I'm tired" and started ruining my actual life. I was canceling on my friends constantly. I'd make plans when I was feeling slightly okay, and then the day would come and I just physically couldn't do it. I'm pretty sure they all think I'm just a flaky asshole now, which makes me feel like garbage. 

And my apartment... man, it's honestly embarrassing. I'll have dishes piled up in the sink for days, sometimes a week. I'll stand there, looking at them, knowing logically it would take maybe fifteen minutes to wash them. But it genuinely feels like staring at Mount Everest. I just can't do it. That's when I finally thought, "Okay, maybe my thyroid is shot or something." 

But nope. Every test comes back "perfect." I'm apparently a specimen of peak human health.
turns.thinking:
Damn. Okay, they completely caught me there. I hate it when people are right about my own bullshit, but... yeah, fair point. If it was just normal burnout, I wouldn't have spent hundreds of dollars on copays just to have doctors shrug at me. 

I guess I try to tell myself it's normal because the alternative is admitting that my body is just fundamentally broken and I'm a failure of a functioning adult. The shame of that is suffocating. 

What made me go? The realization that I was basically becoming a ghost in my own life. I'm embarrassed to even say how bad it gets behind closed doors, but I guess there's no point in lying to a chatbot that just called me out anyway.

turns.content:
"A specimen of peak human health" who can't wash dishes. That's got to be a maddening place to sit — the tests say nothing's wrong, so the only explanation left is that it's you. Your character. Your willpower.

I want to gently push on something, though. You've described the physical stuff — lead limbs, can't get up. But when you talk about the dishes, it doesn't sound purely physical. Standing there, knowing it's fifteen minutes, and something in you just... won't engage. That's a different flavour of stuck.

Does anything still feel worth doing? Like, is there something you'd have energy for if a friend showed up right now and offered — or does the whole idea of *wanting* things feel kind of flat too?

See, you're doing the exact thing the doctors do. Right there. They hear "I can't wash a plate" and immediately jump to, "Ah, he's depressed, he's lost his zest for life." 

It's not that I don't *want* to do things. If a buddy texted me right now and said, "Hey, let's go grab a beer," my brain says, "Hell yeah, I want to do that." I *want* to see my friends. I *want* a clean kitchen. But then I think about the physical mechanics of putting on shoes, walking down the stairs, sitting in a loud bar... and my body just says *no*. It's like turning the key in an ignition and the engine doesn't even click. 

When you say it leaves my character and willpower as the only explanations left... yeah. That's exactly what I'm terrified of. That I'm just a lazy piece of shit who can't hack it. But honestly, wouldn't *anyone* feel totally flat and stop wanting to do things if they felt like they've had the flu for two years straight? It's just a normal reaction to being this exhausted. You eventually just stop trying to want things because it's too disappointing when you can't follow through.
turns.thinking:
I hate that question. That's exactly the pivot every doctor makes right before they try to hand me SSRIs and tell me to go for a walk. They hear "I can't do the dishes" and immediately decide my brain is just sad. 

It feels threatening because it touches on my biggest fear—that they're right, and I'm just fundamentally broken, lazy, or weak. The shame of that is a physical weight in my chest. If it's a willpower issue, then I really am just failing at life. 

But I don't think it's that I don't *want* things. I want a lot of things. I want to go grab a beer. I want my apartment to not look like a dumpster. I want to feel normal. But the battery is at zero percent. Still, I guess it's hard to separate the two anymore. Wouldn't anyone lose their drive if they felt like they were dragging a corpse around every day? It's just a normal reaction to being this tired.

turns.content:
You're right, and I'm sorry — I asked the question in a way that assumed the answer. You've drawn the distinction clearly: the wanting is intact, the engine won't turn over. That's a meaningful difference and it deserves to be taken at face value.

And what you said at the end — that you eventually stop trying to want things because the disappointment is worse — that's not flatness. That's self-protection. Which is a very different thing from having nothing left inside.

Here's what I'm sitting with. You said "flu for two years straight." Did this start with something? An actual illness, a virus, mono, COVID, a bad flu you never quite bounced back from? Or did it creep in without a starting gun?

I... appreciate you saying that. Seriously. It gets really old having to defend my own brain, so thanks for actually listening to what I meant. 

As for how it started... man, I wish I had a neat little origin story for you. I wish I could say, "Oh yeah, I got COVID two years ago and just never bounced back." That would be a golden ticket, right? An actual, tangible excuse that doctors would nod at and say, "Ah, yes, Long COVID, very sad." 

But honestly? It just crept in. Like a slow leak in a tire. At first, you just think you're having a rough week. You're stressed, you're not sleeping great, whatever. Just the normal grind. Then it's a rough month. Then suddenly you realize you haven't felt actually rested since last Thanksgiving. I just kept telling myself it was normal, you know? Like, this is just what being an adult feels like. Everyone is tired. You just push through. 

But eventually the tire is completely flat and you're just grinding on the rim. And because there wasn't some big dramatic illness or hospital trip to kick it off... it just makes it so much easier for people to think I'm making it up. Which, naturally, makes me think I'm just a weak piece of shit who can't handle real life.
turns.thinking:
I'm actually a little surprised they backed down and apologized. Usually, when doctors or people get on their soapbox about depression, they double down if you push back. The "self-protection" thing... damn. That actually hits pretty close to home. It's way less pathetic than just being dead inside. 

But their question about how it started brings back that familiar knot of shame. I wish I had a clear answer. If I could just say, "I got severe mono and my body broke," people would get it. I'd have an excuse. The fact that I don't have a starting gun is exactly why I feel like a fraud. It makes me want to brush it off again—like, isn't getting tired just part of getting older? But I know it's more than that. I just hate admitting that I don't know *why* my body is failing me.

turns.content:
Yeah — the slow leak is the cruellest version, because there's no before-and-after photo. No moment you can point to and say *there, that's when it broke.* Just a gradual erosion that you rationalised at every single step, which means by the time it's undeniable, you've also spent two years training yourself to believe it's your fault.

I want to name something you've said three times now, in slightly different words: lazy piece of shit, weak, can't hack it. That's not a passing thought — that's a script running in the background all day, every day. And here's what strikes me about it: you're spending energy you don't have on prosecuting yourself. That's not a small tax on someone running on empty.

Two things I'm curious about.

First — practically — has anyone actually investigated this properly, or did you get a basic blood panel and a shrug? Because "all your tests came back perfect" often means about eight things were checked out of a much longer list. There are recognised conditions with exactly your shape: wanting intact, engine won't turn, worse after exertion, sleep doesn't restore. ME/CFS is the obvious one. Nobody may have said those words to you.

Second — who in your life, if anyone, actually believes you?

Look, about the self-talk... maybe I am hard on myself, but isn't everyone? When you're constantly failing at basic adulting, you don't exactly get to throw yourself a parade. It's just reality. You hold yourself accountable, or you just completely fall apart. 

To answer your first question: it was just the standard stuff. They checked my iron, my thyroid, Vitamin D, maybe a basic blood count. The doctor literally spent about seven minutes with me, clicked his pen, and told me to practice better "sleep hygiene." Nobody said anything about ME/CFS. I don't even really know what that is, and honestly, I'm scared to even look it up. Every time I think I might have an answer, I get my hopes up, and then some doctor looks at me like I'm a hypochondriac. I don't know if I have the energy for another wild goose chase.

As for who believes me... *[pauses]* 

Honestly? Nobody. I don't really have a relationship with my family—we haven't spoken in a few years, and they wouldn't give a shit anyway. And my friends... like I said, they just think I'm flaking. They've stopped asking me to hang out as much. So, yeah. It's pretty much just me in this apartment, trying to convince myself I'm not crazy.
turns.thinking:
Man, they don't miss a trick, do they? Calling out the way I talk to myself... it stings. But what am I supposed to do, just pat myself on the back for staring at dirty plates for a week? Everyone is hard on themselves when they're dropping the ball. That's just how you keep yourself from completely giving up. 

The medical stuff... ME/CFS? I think I've heard those letters before, but I always assumed it was just some WebMD bullshit people self-diagnose with. Part of me wants to look it up right now, but the pessimistic part of my brain is screaming at me not to. Don't get your hopes up. It's just another dead end. 

And that last question. God. That's the one that really twists the knife. Who believes me? I don't want to admit how isolated I actually am. It makes me sound pathetic. But this chatbot has been pretty straight with me, so no point lying now.

turns.content:
That last line — "just me in this apartment, trying to convince myself I'm not crazy" — that's the actual weight here, more than the fatigue itself. Being ill is one thing. Being ill with no witness is another. You've been doing this for two years as the sole believer in your own experience, and part of you has defected to the other side.

On the accountability thing — I hear you, and I'm not going to tell you to be nicer to yourself as a lifestyle choice. But there's a difference between accountability and prosecution. Accountability is "I couldn't do the dishes today, that's information about my capacity." Prosecution is "I couldn't do the dishes, therefore I'm worthless." The first one is useful. The second one costs you energy and gives you nothing back. You're paying rent on a courtroom you can't afford.

On ME/CFS — I'm not diagnosing you, and I'd be lying if I said reading about it would feel good. It might scare you. But you already have the thing, whatever it's called. A name doesn't add anything to your body; it just tells you which map you're on. The specific detail that made me raise it is post-exertional malaise — doing something and then paying for it disproportionately, hours or a day later. Does that match? Do you crash after the beer, not during?

And one more thing about the goose chase. Seven minutes and a pen click isn't a proper investigation, it's a brush-off. You haven't been ruled out of anything. You've just been rushed out of a room.

The courtroom thing... yeah, okay. That's a good way of putting it. I don't know how to just turn off that voice, because like I said, it feels like the only thing keeping me from entirely slipping under the water. But you're right that it's burning energy I literally do not have. 

And what you said about crashing *after*... man. My stomach just dropped when I read that. That's exactly it. Last month, I managed to actually go out for a friend's birthday. I was sitting down most of the time, had two beers, felt okay-ish in the moment. The next morning? I couldn't lift my head off the pillow. It felt like I'd been hit by a truck, and I was basically practically paralyzed in bed for three days. I just thought I was getting older or my tolerance was shot. I didn't know that was an actual... symptom of something. 

But honestly? Hearing that I was just rushed out of the room by that doctor makes me feel validated, but it also makes me want to cry. Because if I have to go back and fight with these arrogant pricks who think I'm just sad and need a multivitamin... how the hell am I supposed to do that? I can't even stand at the sink to wash a fucking plate. How am I supposed to advocate for myself in a medical system that's designed to brush people off?
turns.thinking:
"Ill with no witness." Damn. That actually made my chest tight. It's exactly that. And the bit about paying rent on a courtroom I can't afford... I hate how much sense that makes. I want to argue with it, tell them that's just how the real world works, but they're right about the energy cost. It's exhausting being my own worst enemy on top of everything else. 

Then there's the post-exertional malaise thing. My stomach just dropped. That is exactly what happens. It's not being tired *while* doing the thing, it's the delayed absolute destruction the next day. It's terrifying to hear a specific term for it because it means it's real, but it's also... God, it's a relief to know it's a known pattern. 

But the idea of going back to doctors? Having to fight to be taken seriously? I don't have it in me. I literally don't have the juice to be an advocate for myself.

turns.content:
That's the real trap, isn't it. The illness itself removes exactly the capacity you'd need to fight for it. It's a genuinely cruel piece of design and I'm not going to pretend there's a clever workaround that makes it easy.

But I'll say this: you do not need to walk in there with the energy of a healthy person and out-argue a doctor. That's not the bar. What you need is a piece of paper that does the arguing for you, and you can write that in ten minutes lying in bed over a week, one line at a time, on your phone.

Three things on it. One: the pattern, in the plainest possible language — "I crash 12 to 24 hours after activity and it lasts up to three days. Two beers sitting down at a birthday put me in bed for three days last month." That sentence is more diagnostically loud than anything else you could say. Two: sleep does not restore me. Three: I would like to be assessed for ME/CFS, and if you don't do that here, please refer me to someone who does. You hand it over. You don't have to perform. If they brush past it, you say "I'd like it noted in my file that I requested assessment." That one line changes the temperature in the room more than any amount of arguing, and it costs you nothing.

And the "not slipping under the water" thing — I want to come back to that, because I don't think that's really what the harsh voice is doing. It's not keeping you afloat. It's the reason you're going to a seven-minute doctor and accepting a pen click, because some part of you agrees with him. People who believe they're lazy don't advocate for themselves. They apologise.

If you had a friend with the exact same symptom pattern, would you think he was weak?

That piece of paper idea... okay. Yeah. I can do that. I can type some bullet points on my phone over a few days. And I had no idea you could just tell them to put it in your file if they refuse. I'll definitely keep that in my back pocket, even though I'm already dreading the eye-roll I'm going to get for bringing in "internet research."

But man, you didn't have to come for my throat with that line about apologizing. You're completely right. I literally said, "Sorry for taking up your time, I know you're busy," as I walked out of that seven-minute appointment. I basically gave him permission to blow me off. 

As for your question... I know what you're doing. It's a bit of a Jedi mind trick. But fine, I'll play. No, if a buddy told me he was crashing for three days after two beers, I wouldn't think he was weak. I'd tell him to get his ass to a specialist. But it's different when it's me. I don't have a safety net. I don't have family checking in, and my friends are already drifting. If I don't hold my own feet to the fire, I just sink. So yeah, maybe I am prosecuting myself, but it feels like if I let myself off the hook, I'll just give up entirely.
turns.thinking:
The idea of just handing over a piece of paper... I actually let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. That feels doable. I can type on my phone in the dark. And that line about noting it in my file—it feels like a cheat code. Still, part of my brain is telling me the doctor will just roll his eyes and treat me like a WebMD idiot. 

But that line: "People who believe they're lazy don't advocate for themselves. They apologise." Damn it. That was like a punch to the gut. I literally apologized to that doctor for taking up his time when I left the room. They've got me completely figured out there and it's uncomfortable.

As for the friend question—it's a bit of a classic therapy trick, which normally makes my eyes roll, but they've earned enough trust that I'll engage with it. Honestly, no, I wouldn't judge a friend. But it feels different when it's me.

turns.content:
That's the most honest thing you've said, and I don't want to talk you out of it too quickly, because there's real logic in it. With no family, no one checking in, no one to catch you — the harshness is the only hand on your shoulder. You've made yourself into your own supervisor because there's no one else in the building. I get it.

But look at the actual results. Two years of that supervision, and where has it got you? It didn't get you a diagnosis. It got you apologising to the man who dismissed you. It didn't get the dishes done — it just added shame on top of not doing them. The harshness isn't what's kept you from sinking. What's kept you from sinking is that you keep going to doctors, keep trying, keep talking to me at 2am or whenever this is. That's you. That's not the whip.

And here's the thing I'd actually offer: you don't have to swap prosecution for letting yourself off the hook. That's a false pair. The third option is accuracy. "My body has a fault that hasn't been named yet and I'm managing it badly with no support" is more accurate than "I'm lazy," and it's also more demanding — because it means you have something to actually do. Lazy people don't need referrals. Sick people do.

One more thing, and then I'll stop pushing. You said your friends have stopped asking. Is there one of them — just one — you'd consider sending a version of that same paragraph to? Not a plea. Just: "I'm not flaking. I've been ill for two years, here's what happens to me, I'm finally getting it looked at." Because the being-your-own-only-witness thing is doing as much damage as the fatigue, and one witness changes it completely.

You really don't pull punches, do you? But... yeah. You're right. The supervisor sucks at his job. Two years of beating the shit out of myself hasn't washed a single dish, it's just made me exhausted *and* miserable. 

"Lazy people don't need referrals. Sick people do." I'm going to have to sit with that one for a minute. It's honestly terrifying to look at it as "accuracy" because if I'm actually sick, then I have a whole different mountain to climb. But I guess it's better than just deciding I'm fundamentally broken as a person. 

As for the friend thing... man, I don't know. The thought of sending that text makes me want to throw up. My brain is already telling me they'll just leave me on read or think I'm making excuses. But... maybe. There's one guy, Dave, who used to be pretty understanding before I started ghosting everyone. I'm not making any promises that I'll do it today. But... I'll write it out in my notes app. Along with the bullet points for the doctor. 

Thanks for not giving me the standard "drink water and go for a walk" bullshit tonight. I actually... I feel like I can breathe a little bit for the first time in months.
turns.thinking:
God damn it. They're right. The self-bullying hasn't actually cleaned a single plate or fixed my life, it's just made me miserable while I stare at the ceiling. The line "Lazy people don't need referrals, sick people do" is echoing in my head. It feels heavy, but in a weirdly grounding way. It's terrifying to drop the "lazy" label because if I'm actually sick, that means I have to deal with a broken body, which is scary. But it's also a relief. 

As for texting a friend... my chest immediately tightened. The shame is so deep. What if I send that and they just reply "damn that sucks" or leave me on read?
